title: How to use Evolving Rep Ranges for Hypertrophy
summary: NH gives a plain-terms tutorial on running evolving rep ranges (e.g. 3x3-5) instead of static schemes (3x3, 5x5). He explains brackets, when to add weight, how bracket size trades intensity against sandbagging, the staircase metaphor for avoiding plateaus, and why evolving sets and rotations are advanced tools most people don't need.
claims: Evolving rep ranges (a bracket like 3x3-5) are superior to static rep ranges (3x3, 5x5) for hypertrophy
NH discovered evolving rep ranges by feel in his own training, not from research; many viewers report doing them without knowing the name
A 3x3-5 means three fixed sets, each of 3, 4 or 5 reps; you cannot go below or above the bracket
Strict brackets exist so you don't drift all over the place, doing 2 reps one day and 20 the next
A typical evolving pattern is reps descending across sets, e.g. 5-4-3, so you keep high-intensity, high-quality tonnage as fatigue lowers your baseline, without sandbagging
If you fall below the bottom of the bracket (e.g. 2 reps on a 3-5), the range or load was set badly; adjust
You don't need to hit the top of the bracket on every set before adding weight; go up whenever realistic, e.g. after 5-4 or 5-4-3, then see if you can still get 3 on set one
The smaller the bracket, the harder it is to progress in weight; the bigger the bracket, the more room to accommodate a new weight
Smaller brackets give higher intensity but more risk of sandbagging; bigger brackets dilute intensity but reduce sandbagging
In his programs, strength work tends to use small brackets and volume work large brackets; the volume brackets make up the bulk of the tonnage
Staircase metaphor: each rep in the bracket is a stair and adding weight is the door at the top; static schemes make you skip stairs and hit a plateau at the door
Evolving rep ranges slow progression at first but keep you in a steady flow with fewer plateaus over the long run
For hypertrophy, a steady stream of gains is better than spikes and plateaus that kill momentum and motivation
Static rep ranges are a stepping stone for completely clueless lifters; convert a 3x3 into a 3x3-5 and it takes about two weeks to figure out
Evolving sets combined with evolving reps (e.g. 1-3 sets of 4-8) can swing tonnage hugely, from one set of 4 to three sets of 8-6-4
Evolving sets and rotations are advanced tools; their flexibility makes programs unstable and requires strong autoregulation skills
Rotating different brackets from workout to workout is unnecessary flexibility; NH doesn't do it
Keep the bracket fixed; changing it whenever you fail to add weight dodges the problem. If you modify it, stick with the modification
8-12 is a sensible volume bracket: if you get 12 on set one you can likely get 11-12 on set two
He likes at least four numbers of breathing room in volume brackets and fewer for intensity, down to three or sometimes two; he never programs 1-2 reps
A bracket must be just right: too big (e.g. 2-20) is useless even though always hittable
Your training needs a balance of larger volume brackets and shorter intensity brackets
If the scheme doesn't work, modify the bracket or modify the load on the bar so it fits
